explanations.explanation: Saul, Israel's king, put his troops under an oath: “Cursed is the man who eats any food before evening…” (1 Samuel 14:24). That's a long day of fighting with nothing in the stomach. The text says the men were in distress, and I believe it. My mustache gets cranky after one skipped snack.

Armor never comes up in Saul's oath. Saul, Israel's king, cursed the man who eats any food before evening (1 Samuel 14:24). The soldiers kept their gear on and their stomachs empty. Nothing in the oath touches their equipment.

Resting isn't what the oath is about. Saul, Israel's king, said, “Cursed is the man who eats any food before evening…” (1 Samuel 14:24). The curse landed on the dinner table, not the cot. I think a rest would have been welcome, but that's not what Saul put in the oath.

The troops entered the forest, and “there was honey on the ground” (1 Samuel 14:25). Honey just lying out there for the taking, with an oath hanging over their heads. That's a tough spot for a hungry soldier. I feel for them.

Manna is the flaky bread that showed up on the ground for Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:31). It's not in this forest, though. Here the troops find honey on the ground (1 Samuel 14:25). Same ground, very different breakfast.

Quail came to Israel's camp in the wilderness, in the evening (Exodus 16:13). This forest is a different scene. The troops find honey on the ground (1 Samuel 14:25). No birds in this story's menu, friend.

The text says it plainly: when they saw the flowing honey, not one of them put his hand to his mouth, “because they feared the oath” (1 Samuel 14:26). Saul's oath had real weight with them. They stayed hungry with the honey right there. That's some serious self-control, and I'm a little jealous.
The text calls it “flowing honey” and says nothing about it being spoiled (1 Samuel 14:26). The reason it gives is the oath. They looked at it and kept their hands down. No sniff test needed.

The text never says Saul was watching. It says they held back “because they feared the oath” (1 Samuel 14:26). The oath was enough to keep their hands down. I think that says a lot about how heavy those words were.

Jonathan, Saul's son, did not walk past. He hadn't heard that his father had bound the people with the oath. So he reached out the end of his staff, dipped it into the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth (1 Samuel 14:27). Jonathan was the one man in that forest who hadn't heard.

Right, he didn't leave it alone. Jonathan, Saul's son, had not heard about the oath, so he dipped the end of his staff into the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth (1 Samuel 14:27). And his eyes brightened. He had no idea he was about to be the only one in the whole forest eating.
A soldier tells Jonathan, Saul's son, “That is why the people are faint” (1 Samuel 14:28). No food all day, and the fighting kept going. Faint is exactly the word. Their strength was running low.
The soldier doesn't say angry. He tells Jonathan, Saul's son, “That is why the people are faint” (1 Samuel 14:28). The oath left them weak, not mad. At least not in what the text tells us.

Scattered isn't the word the soldier uses. He tells Jonathan, Saul's son, that the oath is why “the people are faint” (1 Samuel 14:28). They were still together, just running low on strength. Hungry troops tend to stay close to where the food might be.

That's what he says: “My father has brought trouble to the land” (1 Samuel 14:29). Jonathan, Saul's son, says it right after the soldier tells him about the oath. He points to his own brightened eyes after a little honey. That's quite a thing to say about your own dad.

He did say it. Jonathan, Saul's son, replied, “My father has brought trouble to the land” (1 Samuel 14:29). He then pointed to how his eyes had brightened after tasting a little honey. So this one is true, friend.

Jonathan, Saul's son, says, “How much better it would have been if the troops had eaten freely today from the plunder they took from their enemies!” Then he asks, “Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been much greater?” (1 Samuel 14:30). In his view, fed troops fight better. Hard to argue with that.

Waiting until evening is what Saul's oath demanded (1 Samuel 14:24). Jonathan, Saul's son, says the opposite. He says it would have been better if the troops had eaten freely from the plunder (1 Samuel 14:30). He thinks the waiting hurt them.

The forest isn't Jonathan's point. Jonathan, Saul's son, says it would have been much better if the troops had “eaten freely today from the plunder they took from their enemies” (1 Samuel 14:30). The honey was only his example. His point is about eating.

explanations.answer: Eat meat with the blood still in it
explanations.explanation: The troops rushed greedily to the plunder, took sheep, cattle and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and ate meat with the blood still in it (1 Samuel 14:32). Someone then reported to Saul that the troops were sinning against the LORD (1 Samuel 14:33). Very faint men, a lot of meat, and no patience.

explanations.answer: Drive it all back to their camp
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say they drove it back to camp. It says they slaughtered the animals on the ground and ate meat with the blood still in it (1 Samuel 14:32). They were very faint, and they went straight at the meat. Nobody took the scenic route.

explanations.answer: Burn it as an offering to the LORD
explanations.explanation: They didn't burn it as an offering. They slaughtered the animals on the ground and ate meat with the blood still in it (1 Samuel 14:32). Someone then reported that they were sinning against the LORD (1 Samuel 14:33). The altar comes later, when Saul builds one (1 Samuel 14:35).

That's right. Saul says, “Each man must bring me his ox or his sheep, slaughter them in this place, and then eat. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it” (1 Samuel 14:34). Saul had asked for a large stone to be rolled over (1 Samuel 14:33). That night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there.

It's true, friend. Saul tells the troops, “Each man must bring me his ox or his sheep, slaughter them in this place, and then eat” (1 Samuel 14:34). He also says not to sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it. And that night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there.

Saul built an altar to the LORD. The text adds that it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 14:35). The troops had just slaughtered their oxen there. I'll let the text speak and not add more.
No tower here. The text says Saul built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 14:35). It was the first time he had built one. A tower would have been a lot more construction.

No storehouse, friend. The text says Saul built an altar to the LORD, and it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 14:35). The troops had slaughtered their oxen on the spot. Nobody was saving anything for later.
The priest says, “We must consult God here” (1 Samuel 14:36). Saul had just said let's go after the Philistines by night. The priest asked to stop and ask God first. Good call, and the right order.

The priest never says to wait for daylight. Saul wanted to go down after the Philistines by night, and the priest said, “We must consult God here” (1 Samuel 14:36). The first thing is to ask God. Daylight isn't mentioned.

A sacrifice isn't what the priest asks for. After Saul says he wants to go after the Philistines by night, the priest says, “We must consult God here” (1 Samuel 14:36). He wants them to ask God before they march. Nothing is said about another offering.

Not this time. Saul asked God whether he should go down after the Philistines, “But God did not answer him that day” (1 Samuel 14:37). Saul asked and got silence. I won't guess why, since the text doesn't say.

Right, no answer came. Saul asked God if he should go down after the Philistines and if God would give them into the hand of Israel, “But God did not answer him that day” (1 Samuel 14:37). That's a quiet kind of day. And Saul's next move is to look into how this sin happened.

Saul says, “As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives, even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” (1 Samuel 14:39). Jonathan is Saul's son, and Saul says it before anyone knows who is at fault. Saul didn't know yet that Jonathan had tasted the honey.

Ishvi is one of Saul's sons (1 Samuel 14:49), but he isn't the one Saul names in his oath. Saul says, “even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” (1 Samuel 14:39). Jonathan is the one in the oath. Ishvi isn't mentioned in the story.

Malchishua is one of Saul's sons (1 Samuel 14:49), but Saul names a different one. He says, “even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” (1 Samuel 14:39). Jonathan is the name in the oath. Malchishua isn't part of this scene.
Not a word. After Saul swears that whoever sinned must die, even his son Jonathan, “not one of the troops said a word” (1 Samuel 14:39). A whole army and total quiet. I think that's a heavy silence.
The text says otherwise. After Saul's oath, even if it is his son Jonathan, “not one of the troops said a word” (1 Samuel 14:39). So the troops stayed quiet. This one is true, friend.

Saul asked the LORD to answer with Urim if the fault was with him or Jonathan, and with Thummim if it was with the men of Israel. Then “Jonathan and Saul were selected, but the people were cleared of the charge” (1 Samuel 14:41). So the people were cleared. The next step is a lot between the two of them.

The men of Israel were the ones cleared. The text says, “Jonathan and Saul were selected, but the people were cleared of the charge” (1 Samuel 14:41). So the selected side was Saul and Jonathan. The troops can breathe.

There was an answer. The text says, “Jonathan and Saul were selected, but the people were cleared of the charge” (1 Samuel 14:41). God had been silent earlier (1 Samuel 14:37), and then one side was selected. It was the side with Saul and Jonathan.
It didn't fall on Saul. Saul said, “Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan.” And “Jonathan was selected” (1 Samuel 14:42). The lot landed on his son. I think that's a hard moment for any father.

Right, the lot fell on Jonathan. After Saul said, “Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan,” the text says, “And Jonathan was selected” (1 Samuel 14:42). Saul had sworn that whoever sinned must die, even if it was Jonathan. Now his son was the one selected.

explanations.answer: He swears Jonathan will surely die
explanations.explanation: Saul says, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!” (1 Samuel 14:44). Jonathan had just told him he only tasted a little honey. Saul doubled down on his oath. That's a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: He says the oath doesn't count for him
explanations.explanation: Saul says the opposite. He answers, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!” (1 Samuel 14:44). The oath still stands, and it lands on Jonathan, Saul's own son. Nobody gets an exception in this scene.

explanations.answer: He tells the priest to decide it
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Saul handing it to the priest. Saul himself declares, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!” (1 Samuel 14:44). The priest spoke earlier about consulting God (1 Samuel 14:36), but here it's Saul's own oath. He didn't pass it along.

explanations.answer: He brought a great deliverance for Israel
explanations.explanation: The people say, “Must Jonathan die…he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel? Never!” (1 Samuel 14:45). They add, “for with God's help he has accomplished this today.” The troops finally speak up. They point to what Jonathan did for Israel.

explanations.answer: He promised never to do it again
explanations.explanation: No promise like that is in the text. The people say, “…he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel?” (1 Samuel 14:45). Their reason is what Jonathan did for Israel. They didn't mention any promise.

explanations.answer: He offered a sacrifice for his sin
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a sacrifice from Jonathan. The people say, “…he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel?” (1 Samuel 14:45). Their reason is that deliverance, with God's help. Nothing about an offering.

The text says, “So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die” (1 Samuel 14:45). The troops had stayed silent earlier (1 Samuel 14:39). This time they spoke up, and it saved Jonathan. Good thing they found their voices.
They didn't punish him. The text says, “So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die” (1 Samuel 14:45). They stood up against Saul's oath for Jonathan's sake. He lived.
Nobody was banished. The text says, “So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die” (1 Samuel 14:45). Jonathan stayed, and he lived. The people stepped in for him.

The text says, “Then Saul gave up his pursuit of the Philistines” (1 Samuel 14:46). Earlier he wanted to go down after them by night (1 Samuel 14:36). Now he stops. The Philistines went back to their own land.

That was Saul's plan earlier. He said, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night…” (1 Samuel 14:36). But in the end the text says, “Saul gave up his pursuit of the Philistines” (1 Samuel 14:46). So no chase through the night.

No peace deal is mentioned. The text says Saul “gave up his pursuit of the Philistines, and the Philistines returned to their own land” (1 Samuel 14:46). Saul stopped chasing them. And the war with the Philistines was fierce all the days of Saul (1 Samuel 14:52).
